summary: Epalrestat is an oral aldose reductase inhibitor used (mainly in Japan and parts of Asia) to treat the symptoms of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. By blocking the polyol pathway it reduces intracellular sorbitol accumulation thought to contribute to nerve damage. It is taken before meals and is not approved by the US FDA.
indications: Improvement of subjective neuropathic symptoms (numbness, pain, paraesthesia) and abnormal nerve function associated with diabetic peripheral neuropathy

dosage.d: 50 mg three times daily before meals
dosage.n: Take before breakfast, lunch and dinner

admin: Maintain good glycaemic control alongside therapy
Continue regular use; benefit is symptomatic and gradual
Inform patients urine may be discoloured (reddish-brown)
moa: Epalrestat reversibly inhibits aldose reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of the polyol pathway. In hyperglycaemia this enzyme converts excess glucose to sorbitol, which accumulates in nerve tissue causing osmotic and oxidative damage. By inhibiting aldose reductase, epalrestat reduces sorbitol and fructose accumulation and improves nerve conduction and symptoms in diabetic neuropathy.
preg: Not recommended in pregnancy; safety has not been established. Avoid unless clearly necessary and no safer alternative exists.
lact: Avoid during breastfeeding; safety in lactation has not been established. Discontinue nursing or the drug.
renal: Limited data; use with caution in renal impairment. No well-defined dose adjustment is specified.
hepatic: Hepatic dysfunction (elevated transaminases, jaundice) has been reported. Monitor liver function and use with caution in hepatic impairment; discontinue if significant liver injury occurs.

moderate: Other potentially hepatotoxic drugs (additive liver risk)
minor: Antidiabetic agents (no direct interaction but monitor glycaemic control)
interactions.food: Taken before meals; food may affect absorption
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol - may add hepatic stress and worsen glycaemic control
interactions.diagnostics: Causes reddish-brown discolouration of urine; may elevate liver enzymes

emergency: Acute liver failure (jaundice, marked LFT rise)

counsel: Your urine may turn a reddish-brown colour - this is harmless
Keep blood sugar well controlled for best benefit

Symptom improvement is gradual; continue as prescribed
pk: Symptomatic benefit develops gradually over weeks of regular use
Plasma peak approximately 1-3 hours after an oral dose
Store at room temperature, protected from light and moisture
pearls: Not FDA-approved; used mainly in Japan, India and parts of Asia for diabetic neuropathy (data drawn from SmPC/regional labels and BNF-type references, not US FDA label)
Harmless reddish-brown urine discolouration is a recognised effect - reassure patients
Works by blocking the polyol pathway (aldose reductase) implicated in diabetic nerve damage
Hepatotoxicity is the key safety concern - monitor liver enzymes
Best results require concurrent tight glycaemic control
missed: Take the missed dose before your next meal if remembered soon; if it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed one and resume your usual schedule. Do not take a double dose.
overdose: Experience with overdose is limited. Manage supportively with attention to gastrointestinal symptoms and liver function; there is no specific antidote.
